name: ziyang Yan
body:
Thank you for sharing your thoughts. After a year of vibe coding, I’ve come to see using AI as something like choosing between a horse-drawn carriage and a car. Instead of spending all our time debating which is better, I think we should focus on learning to drive well: staying in control and making sure we’re heading where we actually want to go.

At one point, the flood of knowledge AI opened up to me was overwhelming. I spent three months caught up in a whirlwind of conversations and ideas with it. As AI has become more capable, it has gotten much better at solving problems with clear objectives. What you describe as the work beyond problem-solving seems to me to be about framing problems and developing approaches in response to real-world situations.

I tend to see research as moving in two broad directions: advancing technology itself, and applying it to practical problems. In tribology, where I work, AI has led to more papers in areas where the questions and boundaries were already blurry. But to me, research is fundamentally about separating what is true from what is false and staying grounded in facts. Whether we’re developing technology or applying it, if our work loses touch with objective reality, we risk ending up wearing the emperor’s new clothes.

This also makes me think that, whether we’re talking about AI or a broader technological revolution, what we ultimately need is substantive change. Small compromises in how we do research won’t be enough.

For example, in the agent system I use, there’s a skill called “goal.” It’s meant to help turn a conversation with the user into a clear, structured objective. But the agent still struggles to carry that objective through to completion. I once tried to get an agent to work continuously on an ambitious task for more than 72 hours. No matter what I tried, it would eventually get stuck somewhere.

It feels a bit like finding our way through a maze. We spot a signpost, mark where we’ve been, and keep moving. Sometimes we go around in circles; sometimes we find a way out. That’s how I see AI at the moment, and our own attempts to learn how to use it.

But I’ve also noticed a serious problem: how easily we become dependent on these tools. Whenever I discover a new tool, I tend to hand tasks over to it without thinking much about it. Yet it has its own limits, and it doesn’t approach the work the way I would. So I often don’t get the outcome I was aiming for.

As AI companies push the technology forward, especially toward practical applications, I feel that some capabilities are being developed at the expense of others. We put enormous effort into mathematical reasoning, for example, while overlooking basic conventions in how language is used. That’s a gap that skills don’t seem able to close. Perhaps it’s a kind of tunnel vision produced by the way more advanced capabilities are trained. Whatever the reason, AI’s behavior and responses increasingly resemble those of a person. But this “person” isn’t a baby. It feels more like an incomplete person, half an expert, or perhaps an expert with tunnel vision.
